opus-5.5.text:
I think in-context learning is one of the most underappreciated capabilities we've seen emerge from large models, and in some ways it's also one of the least understood.

The basic idea is simple: instead of updating a model's weights through training, you give it examples, instructions, or experience directly in its context, and it adapts its behavior on the fly. When we first saw this working at scale, it was surprising, because nobody explicitly trained these models to "learn" at inference time. It emerged from predicting the next token over enormous amounts of data.

For me, coming from a reinforcement learning background, the promise is really about adaptation. In RL, we've always cared about agents that can deal with new situations, new tasks, new environments. Traditionally, that meant you had to go back and retrain, which is slow and expensive. With in-context learning, you have a system that can, in principle, pick up a new task from a handful of demonstrations, or adjust its strategy based on feedback it gets during an interaction. That starts to look a lot more like how humans operate. You don't retrain your brain every time someone shows you a new tool. You watch, you try, you get feedback, and you adjust.

Where I think it gets really exciting is when you combine it with agents acting over long horizons. If a model can take actions, observe outcomes, and keep that history in context, then in-context learning becomes a kind of fast inner loop of learning, sitting on top of the slow outer loop of pretraining and RL fine-tuning. That's a very powerful structure. It's a bit like meta-learning, which people in the RL community have chased for years, except now it's happening at a scale and generality we couldn't really reach before.

That said, I'd be careful about overstating where we are. Context windows are finite, models don't always use long context well, and there's a real question about how much of what looks like learning is actually retrieval of patterns the model already knows. The open challenge is getting systems that genuinely accumulate new knowledge and skills through experience, reliably, over long periods. I think that's one of the key steps toward much more capable and autonomous agents, and it's a big part of what makes this moment in the field so interesting.

r001.rationale: It says a system can pick up a new task from a handful of demonstrations supplied in context.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from actions, observations, and feedback, but says genuinely accumulating new knowledge through experience remains an open challenge. It does not clearly identify interaction as a means to acquire knowledge beyond what the model already knows.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the most honest way to put it is that in-context learning is the thing that surprised me most about large language models, and I spent years working on systems that were supposed to be the pinnacle of learning from experience.

With AlphaGo and the systems that followed, the learning happened in training. You run millions of self-play games, you update the weights, and what you get at the end is a network that is extremely strong at exactly one thing. If you wanted it to play a new game, you went back and trained again. The knowledge lived entirely in the parameters, and there was no mechanism for the system to pick something up in the moment.

What in-context learning changes is that the model can adapt without anyone touching the weights. You show it a few examples, or you describe a task it has never seen in that exact form, and it adjusts its behavior right there in the forward pass. In a sense the network has learned a learning algorithm, and that algorithm runs at inference time. That is a qualitatively different capability from anything we had in the reinforcement learning era.

The promise, to me, has a few parts. The first is generality. You stop building one model per task and start building a model that can be instructed. The second is speed of iteration. A researcher or a product team can try an idea in minutes instead of weeks, because adaptation is now a matter of what you put in the prompt. And the third, which I find most interesting, is that it opens a path toward systems that improve through interaction. If a model can take feedback, examples, and intermediate results in its context and genuinely use them, then you have the beginnings of a system that gets better over the course of a problem rather than only between training runs.

I would add one caution. In-context learning is powerful, but it is not the same as durable learning. Whatever the model picks up in context disappears when the context does. So I see it as one half of the picture. The other half is still about how we train these systems, how we use search and reinforcement learning to make them better reasoners, and how we eventually close the loop so that what a model discovers in context can feed back into what it knows permanently. The combination of those two things is where I think the real promise lies.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can adapt to a task by being shown a few examples in its prompt, without changing its weights.

r002.rationale: It describes improving through interaction using feedback and examples in context, but does not clearly identify interaction with the environment as the means of acquiring knowledge beyond what the system already stores.

astra-6.text:
I think the promise is that a system can learn from what’s happening in the conversation without us having to retrain it. You can give it examples, explain a new task, or provide feedback, and it can use that context to change how it behaves.

That’s a very powerful idea because we can’t anticipate every situation a model will encounter during training. We want systems that can adapt when they encounter something new. In-context learning gives us a way to do that: the interaction itself becomes part of how you teach the system.

The question is how far that can go. Can it pick up a genuinely new concept from a few examples? Can it use feedback reliably over a longer task? And can it carry useful lessons forward? I think that’s where a lot of the promise lies.

r001.rationale: The response says a system can use examples and an explanation of a new task in the conversation to change its behavior, and explicitly discusses learning from a few examples.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from conversation context and feedback, but does not identify interaction with the environment as a way to gain knowledge beyond what the system already stores.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing about in-context learning is that a model can adapt to a task through the interaction itself. You can give it a few examples, explain what you want, or correct a mistake, and it can use that information without changing its underlying parameters.

That opens up a different way of building useful systems. You don’t necessarily have to train a separate model for every task; you can give a general model the right context. The question is how far that can go—whether the system can reliably extract the underlying idea from what you show it and apply it to a new situation, rather than just follow the surface pattern.

r001.rationale: It says a model can adapt to a task by receiving a few examples in its context.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting through prompts and corrections, but does not say interaction with the environment lets the system acquire knowledge beyond what it already stores.
